risks.message: 4 SQL statements executed on every iteration of this LOOP (lines 38, 60, 62, 65): one database round-trip each per row. Prefer set-based statements.

recommendations.message: Keep joins, aggregates, CTEs and bulk DML as parameterized SQL.
Collapse per-row statements inside loops into one set-based statement.

architectural_decisions.decision: The cursor loop (4 SQL statements per iteration) was collapsed into one set-based statement using CTEs: a LATERAL join picks the applicable fee row (ORDER BY vigente_de DESC LIMIT 1, same as the original SELECT ... INTO), and data-modifying CTEs perform the balance update, the TARIFA inserts, the per-transaction audit rows and the final batch audit row.
architectural_decisions.rationale: Semantics allow it: no row locking, no procedural side effects between iterations, and the final audit totals are aggregates of the per-row fees. This removes the high-severity N+1 risk while keeping all relational logic in SQL.

architectural_decisions.decision: Each PL/pgSQL assignment to a NUMERIC(18,2) variable is reproduced in SQL with an explicit CAST(... AS NUMERIC(18,2)): first after GREATEST(valor*percentual/100.0, minimo), then again after the CASE multiplier (1.10 / 1.0 / 0.90).
architectural_decisions.rationale: PL/pgSQL rounds on every assignment to a NUMERIC(p,s) variable; a single combined expression would round only once and produce different values. PostgreSQL's CAST to NUMERIC rounds half away from zero, exactly matching the PL/pgSQL assignment behaviour.

architectural_decisions.decision: The per-row UPDATE contas was replaced by an UPDATE ... FROM (SELECT conta_origem_id, SUM(taxa) ... GROUP BY conta_origem_id), so each account is debited exactly once with the sum of its fees.
architectural_decisions.rationale: UPDATE ... FROM applies at most one source row per target row; several transactions of the same day can hit the same account, so the source must be aggregated by the target key.

architectural_decisions.decision: No commit/rollback is issued; the caller owns the transaction, as in the original procedure.
architectural_decisions.rationale: The PL/pgSQL procedure does not manage transactions; the whole batch must be atomic exactly as before.

architectural_decisions.decision: Every occurrence of :p_data_referencia in a polymorphic position (DATE() comparison, date comparisons, jsonb_build_object value) is written as CAST(:p_data_referencia AS DATE).
architectural_decisions.rationale: asyncpg cannot infer types of bind parameters in polymorphic positions; CAST(:x AS type) is used instead of :x::type because SQLAlchemy does not recognise :name as a bind when :: follows.

warnings: The original cursor reads transacoes without any row lock (no FOR UPDATE); the port preserves this, so concurrent modifications between statement execution are handled by PostgreSQL's statement-level snapshot, same as the original cursor snapshot.

The final audit row's 'total_taxas' is the exact sum of the already-rounded per-row fees (each fee was rounded to 2 decimal places before accumulation in the original), so no additional rounding step is needed; SUM over 2-decimal values is exact.
The original CASE for 'TRANSFERENCIA' re-assigns v_taxa unchanged (v_taxa := v_taxa); the port multiplies by 1.0 and re-rounds, which is a no-op numerically.

Rows whose transaction type has no applicable fee row, or whose conta_origem_id is NULL, are skipped exactly as the original IF/CONTINUE and IF v_origem IS NOT NULL logic did; they are counted neither in 'transacoes' nor in 'total_taxas' of the batch audit row.
The routine has no RAISE statements, so no typed exception paths exist beyond the defensive FeeBatchError class; the original procedure also had no EXCEPTION blocks, so no savepoints are required.

If the 'taxas' table ever contains duplicate rows with the same vigente_de for a tipo_operacao, the LATERAL LIMIT 1 pick is non-deterministic in both the original and the port (same ORDER BY); consider adding a tiebreaker index/column.
